newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG stocks jump on relief at peaceful end to crisis.
newsitem.headline: PNG stocks jump on relief at peaceful end to crisis.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's Australian-listed stocks rallied in active trade on Thursday as foreign investors breathed a sigh of relief at the apparent peaceful resolution of the Pacific nation's political crisis.

Analysts said investors welcomed Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan's decision late on Wednesday to step aside, which calmed an explosive situation and should allow a peaceful transition to a new government.
"Everyone is relieved that the parliamentary process actually worked and that we didn't go into a period of military control," said ABN AMRO Hoare Govett mining research head David Walker.
"The expectation that the mid-year elections can be brought forward and that there can be an orderly resolution of the impasse has been accepted well," Walker said.
Chan stood down on Wednesday after pressure mounted for his resignation over the hiring of mercenaries to end an uprising on copper-rich Bougainville island.
Papua New Guinea stocks listed in Australia -- the country does not have its own stock market -- rallied in late trade on news of Chan's decision and firmed again on Thursday.

Mining investment group Orogen Minerals Ltd, which is 51 percent owned by the Papua New Guinea government, closed on Thursday up eight cents at A$3.10 (US$2.45). Oil producer and explorer Oil Search Ltd, the largest of the pure Papua New Guinea stocks listed in Australia, ended 13 cents higher at A$2.70.

Lihir Gold Ltd, which is developing one of the world's largest gold deposits, rose two cents to A$2.15. Retailer and trader Collins and Leahy Ltd closed up 25 cents at A$3.50, and Bougainville Copper Ltd firmed five cents at 60 cents.
However, analysts said Papua New Guinea stocks were unlikely to immediately recover all their losses of the past 10 days as the makeup and policies of the caretaker government were unknown.
Investor confidence remained bruised by images of street riots and the standoff between army and government.
"It's positive that Chan has (stepped aside) and it should calm the situation up there somewhat," said ANZ Securities gold analyst David Kauler.
"However, it's clear Papua New Guinea is now in election mode and there's still a period of three to six months of uncertainty ahead," Kauler said.
He expected a period of volatility as some investors looked for cheap buying opportunities.
Analysts also said the resolution of the political crisis could bring higher taxes for foreign miners.
ABN AMRO's Walker said the new government would have to consider increasing taxes, possibly including the 1.25 percent mining royalty, to overcome a chronic budget deficit.
However, a return to stability at the same time as the controversy over the supposedly huge Busang gold deposit in nearby Indonesia had also created a window of opportunity.
"Papua New Guinea, having overcome its immediate problems, has really got to settle down and project an image of stability, because there will be capital funds coming out of Indonesia," said Walker.
